Development of an Intelligent Web System for Analyzing Scientific Articles for Compliance with Scientific Conference Requirements and Generating Recommendations. This report prepares the first probationary-period submission due on 24 October 2026 at 18:00 Asia/Almaty. The project assists authors in checking a manuscript against explicitly supplied conference requirements and produces evidence-linked recommendations.

The current deliverable is an analysis and design package with an interactive mock prototype. The complete application, external AI integration and empirical benchmark have not been implemented. No stakeholder interviews, supervisor approval, individual teammate contributions or measured performance are claimed.

Conference requirements combine document structure, measurable limits and qualitative expectations. Authors must locate these rules, inspect a PDF or DOCX and explain what needs revision. The working problem hypothesis is that a reusable, criterion-level checking workflow can reduce missed requirements and make revision more systematic. Its local relevance still requires direct user evidence; literature and product pages alone do not establish demand among our intended users.

Primary users are students and early-career researchers preparing conference submissions. A supervisor may inspect the exported results, but the MVP does not require a separate supervisor account or conference-administration role. Initially, validation focuses on English-language, text-based manuscripts and explicit criteria; support for Russian or Kazakh is a later evaluation decision.

The aim is to design and evaluate a locally runnable web system that identifies supported formal and semantic mismatches between a manuscript and user-confirmed requirements, explains findings with source evidence, and recommends concrete revisions. Objectives are to specify requirements; compare related approaches; normalize documents and criteria; implement deterministic and LLM-assisted checks; preserve evidence and run versions; and measure accuracy, coverage, latency and usefulness against declared baselines.

The review uses 17 sources: 13 research publications or research reports and 4 primary technical/product sources. Twelve research entries are from 2023-2025; the 2020 RAG paper is retained as a foundational work. Preprints and technical reports are explicitly labelled. Search terms combined manuscript evaluation, conference compliance, rubric-based evaluation, LLM-as-a-Judge, PDF parsing, attribution, document understanding and retrieval-augmented generation. Primary publication pages, author repositories and official documentation were consulted on 22 October 2026.

Selection favoured work that affects one of four decisions: the reliability of AI feedback, criterion-level evaluation, document conversion, or evidence selection. Vendor pages were used only for documented features. This is a focused engineering review, not a systematic review; it does not claim exhaustive retrieval or a meta-analysis.

Liang et al. [S01] support the potential usefulness of generated manuscript feedback, whereas Zhou et al. [S02] show why helpfulness must not be confused with reliable technical judgment. SEA [S03] offers a staged scientific-review framework; Li et al. [S12] further motivate evaluation of contextual grounding and criticism. For this project, the resulting design choice is to verify bounded criteria and show evidence rather than issue an overall scientific acceptance score.

MT-Bench [S04], G-Eval [S05] and Prometheus [S06] motivate explicit criteria and structured judgments, while exposing transfer and bias concerns. Their tasks are different from conference compliance; their reported performance cannot be reused as our accuracy. Attribute or Abstain [S08] motivates inspectable evidence and abstention. A source anchor must therefore be both structurally valid and semantically supportive; JSON validity alone [D04] cannot demonstrate either correctness or usefulness.

Nougat [S09], Docling [S10] and GROBID [D03] provide different routes to structured scholarly text. The project must measure conversion errors separately, because a missed section in extraction can become a false compliance failure. Lost in the Middle [S07] motivates positional sensitivity tests. RAG [S13] and Self-RAG [S11] explain retrieval approaches, but retrieval can omit evidence needed for exhaustive checking. A vector database is therefore an option to test, not an assumed requirement.

S01 | Liang et al. (2023)
LLM manuscript feedback can be useful, but utility is not equivalent to correct conference compliance.
Retrospective review overlap and researcher perceptions do not validate an arbitrary checklist.
Use feedback as assistance and validate every criterion on an independently annotated set.

S02 | Zhou, Chen and Yu (2024)
Review generation and score prediction expose limitations in critical and long-document reasoning.
Scores and fluent reviews can conceal factual mistakes.
Separate formal checks from semantic judgments; permit insufficient_evidence and human review.

S03 | Yu et al. (2024)
SEA separates standardization, evaluation and consistency analysis in scientific reviewing.
Its training and review-generation setting differs from user-supplied conference criteria.
Use a staged pipeline and check consistency between a finding and the cited manuscript text.

S04 | Zheng et al. (2023)
LLM judges approximate some human preferences but have position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases.
Chat-assistant preference agreement is not manuscript-compliance accuracy.
Evaluate criterion order sensitivity, repeated-run stability and agreement with human labels.

S05 | Liu et al. (2023)
Explicit evaluation criteria and structured judging can improve alignment in NLG tasks.
Summarization and dialogue findings do not establish validity for scientific paper assessment.
Use an explicit rubric and structured outputs; retain a separate human reference.

S06 | Kim et al. (2024)
Custom rubrics support fine-grained feedback and evaluation.
Rubric-conditioned response evaluation and reference answers differ from checking unseen conference rules.
Store criterion definitions and rubric versions; benchmark a fixed rubric rather than one global score.

S07 | Liu et al. (2024)
Performance can depend on the location of relevant evidence in a long input.
The experiments study retrieval tasks, not this project or every future model.
Preserve section anchors; test evidence moved to the beginning, middle and end.

S08 | Buchmann, Liu and Gurevych (2024)
Attribution makes long-document responses more verifiable; evidence quality remains task dependent.
A citation alone does not guarantee support for a complex claim.
Validate quoted spans and ask human annotators whether evidence supports each finding.

S09 | Blecher et al. (2023)
Visual document recognition converts academic PDF content into structured markup.
A neural parser may introduce recognition errors; reliable formatting checks require retained layout data.
Compare layout-aware conversion with plain extraction and explicitly flag unsupported scanned files.

S10 | Auer et al. (2024)
Layout and table models support structured local PDF conversion.
The v1 report does not validate the current package on our PDF/DOCX corpus.
Pilot Docling as a parser adapter; measure heading and reading-order accuracy on representative files.

S11 | Asai et al. (2024)
Retrieval decisions and critique can improve grounded generation in studied tasks.
The trained retrieval-reflection framework is not equivalent to merely adding a vector database.
Treat retrieval as an experimental extension; start with explicit section evidence and compare baselines.

S12 | Li et al. (2025)
Structured and descriptive reviews can coexist with weak critical reasoning and contextual grounding.
Review-generation benchmarks differ from deterministic and semantic compliance checks.
Evaluate correctness, unsupported claims and actionable feedback separately from writing quality.

S13 | Lewis et al. (2020)
Combining parametric generation with retrieved context establishes a retrieval-augmented approach.
Knowledge-intensive QA results do not guarantee exhaustive detection of missing manuscript elements.
Retain as a foundational reference and compare retrieval with full-context and rules-only approaches.

The project gap is an engineering combination to be validated: author-confirmed conference criteria, explicit formal/semantic check boundaries, traceable PDF/DOCX evidence and reproducible local evaluation. Existing products already cover configurable checks and critique, so universal novelty or superiority is not claimed. The complete source matrix and URLs are provided in the repository.

Four relevant systems are compared across the same eight criteria: Penelope.ai [D01], Paperpal Preflight [D02], SEA [S03] and the Liang et al. scientific-feedback pipeline [S01]. The last two are research systems rather than equivalent commercial products. This distinction is necessary when interpreting reproducibility and feature coverage.

These are source-based comparisons, not hands-on tests. Not established means the reviewed source does not substantiate a capability; it does not prove that capability is absent. The proposed system should be justified by the local user need and evaluated implementation, not by unsupported negative claims about competitors. A promising design emphasis is an author-editable conference rubric with criterion-level provenance and explicit uncertainty.

Six technical decisions are compared with three reasonable alternatives each. Vue 3, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Pinia, Go, REST and Docker Compose are already specified in the team justification. Storage, parsing, model choice and evidence selection remain proposals until the team and supervisor review them.
Plain PDF text plus DOCX parser
Backend: Go selected in team justification; keep orchestration, storage and validation here. Python remains a possible internal parser adapter, not a replacement backend.
Data storage: Propose PostgreSQL for relational versioned runs; SQLite is a simpler local alternative. Decision requires pilot and supervisor review; no database implemented yet.
Document conversion: Propose Docling pilot for layout; compare GROBID on scholarly PDFs. Plain text baseline cannot verify fonts/margins. [S09,S10,D03]
Evaluation strategy: Propose hybrid checks: deterministic for counts/structure, LLM for semantic criteria; compare both baselines. [S02,S05,D04]
Component interaction: REST/JSON selected in justification; easier boundary inspection and language-independent parser interface. No latency advantage claimed.
Evidence selection: Start with section/block selection and explicit limits; compare full-context baseline; vector retrieval only if tests show need. [S07,S08,S11,S13]

The OpenAI model identifier is configured through the server environment and recorded in every run. Select an available model that supports the chosen structured-output workflow after a small pilot; this report does not lock a model, token price or context limit. There is no paid model call in the prototype and no purchased cloud hosting. Local deployment still requires internet and an API key for external AI analysis; local startup does not mean the AI model runs offline.

Parser dependencies should remain behind a stable interface. A Python adapter is a proposed implementation route for Docling, while Go remains the application backend. Keep a rules-only mode for baseline evaluation and for checks supported without an LLM. A pilot must establish extraction quality before adding OCR or retrieval complexity.

Requirements use Must, Should and Could priorities. The current MVP has 12 functional and 8 non-functional requirements. Every requirement has a test identifier and an acceptance criterion. Numerical limits below are proposed engineering targets, not measured achievements, and require review against stakeholder evidence.
Upload a scientific paper in PDF or DOCX
A valid supported file at or below 20 MB creates a document ID; unsupported, malformed, encrypted or oversize files return an explicit error.
Extract document text and retain provenance
Text blocks have stable block IDs, reading order, section labels and PDF pages where available; DOCX uses paragraph/table anchors, not fabricated page numbers.
A user can paste criteria or attach PDF/DOCX; original wording and source identifiers are retained.
User can edit criterion wording, category, threshold, priority and applicability; analysis uses the confirmed version.
Every applicable criterion returns pass, fail or insufficient_evidence; excluded criteria return not_applicable with a reason. No criterion silently disappears.
Each evaluable finding includes criterion ID, explanation, valid source anchors and an actionable recommendation when appropriate; invalid anchors are rejected.
Keep formal and semantic checks distinct
Results identify engine=rule or engine=llm and state unsupported layout checks; plain text is never used to certify font size or margins.
Restarting the local system preserves document metadata, criterion versions, results and run configuration; a run can be reopened.
An analysis can be downloaded as JSON with document hash, criterion version and model/prompt configuration; PDF export is a later enhancement.
A new manuscript creates a new document version and run; the earlier result remains identifiable.
Timeout, refusal, invalid JSON and provider errors produce a retryable failure state; no successful assessment is invented.
Before external analysis, UI explains that extracted content goes to the configured provider; user can delete stored files and results.
Each run records document hash, confirmed criteria, parser/model ID and version, prompt/schema version, sampling settings and timestamp.
All accepted results satisfy the shared JSON schema; each criterion occurs once; all cited block IDs exist and quoted text matches source text after documented whitespace normalization.
API keys only in server environment; examples contain placeholders; uploads use generated paths and size/type validation; external content cannot execute instructions or tools.
On a documented supported Docker environment, one Docker Compose command starts the implemented services after environment setup; smoke checks are documented. Target for implementation stage.

Report p50/p95 latency, provider tokens and estimated cost per run on specified hardware and corpus; proposed target p95 <= 120 s for <= 10 text-PDF pages and <= 10 criteria, to be revised after pilot.

Evaluate >= 20 rights-cleared manuscripts with 8-12 criteria each using a frozen test split; report macro-F1, abstention coverage and supported-evidence rate. These are planned measurements, not achieved results.
Core controls support keyboard navigation, visible focus and labeled error/status messages on desktop and narrow screens.
UI and reports distinguish unavailable OCR/layout checks from checked failures, and demonstrate that unknown evidence is not treated as a pass.

Four result states avoid conflating absent evidence with compliance: pass, fail, insufficient_evidence and not_applicable. A document with no extractable text must fail the extraction stage rather than receive a compliant result. Criteria that require unsupported visual metadata remain explicitly unverified. Ambiguous requirements must be confirmed by the user before being treated as executable rules.

The versioned result contract requires criterion_id, status, engine, explanation, evidence and recommendation. Evidence contains a block_id and a matching quote; page numbers are nullable and derived from the PDF parser, while DOCX uses stable paragraph/table anchors. The backend checks completeness, uniqueness, schema conformance and anchor validity before presenting a result.

The context, use-case and component diagrams describe the same local single-user system. The author operates a Vue client; the Go application coordinates storage, document parsing, rule checks and external LLM requests. The parser and judge are replaceable adapters. The external AI provider is outside the local trust boundary. No separate admin system or multi-user authentication is assumed for the first local MVP.

The backend validates an upload and computes its content hash, stores the file under a generated path, extracts structured blocks, and displays extraction warnings. Proposed REST resources are POST /api/documents, POST /api/criteria-sets, POST /api/analyses, GET /api/analyses/{id}, GET /api/analyses and DELETE /api/documents/{id}. Runs may expose queued, processing, completed and failed states; the first implementation can use a local worker without a separate distributed queue. Schema examples and data-model notes are included as editable repository files.

Uploaded article and requirement text are untrusted data: instructions embedded in them must not change the system prompt, trigger tools or override the rubric. Do not execute document macros. Validate model-generated anchors against extraction output; keep unsupported checks visible. Store keys server-side and exclude raw private manuscripts from Git. These controls are requirements to implement and test, not security guarantees already achieved.

The prototype is a UX artefact and does not establish usability or analysis quality. Ask actual target users to complete one task and record time, confusion and comments; the relevance interview kit includes this activity.

RQ1: does a hybrid rule-plus-LLM pipeline identify supported criterion violations more accurately than rules alone? RQ2: does criterion-level evidence improve the rate of supported explanations compared with one unconstrained whole-document prompt? RQ3: what are the cost, latency and stability trade-offs under fixed files and criteria? These questions remain untested.

Baseline B0 runs deterministic checks only and abstains on semantic criteria. Baseline B1 uses one whole-document LLM prompt with the same available model and documents, a fixed criterion list and no staged evidence validation. Proposed method B2 uses confirmed criteria, deterministic supported checks, section-level evidence and schema/anchor validation. Keep prompts and token limits versioned; compare each method on its eligible criterion types and report common subsets separately.

Plan at least 20 rights-cleared text-based English manuscripts with 8-12 criteria each. Use permitted public papers or author-consented drafts, plus explicitly synthetic controlled variants. Preserve base-document groups so variants never cross development/test boundaries. A proposed split is 8 development and 12 held-out documents. Freeze test labels before tuning prompts. Use two annotators; record initial labels, disagreements and adjudicated labels. Synthetic variants test known violations but cannot substitute for evaluation on real papers.

Create criteria from real, dated conference guidelines, respecting applicable reuse terms. Include missing required sections, abstract-length violations, absent limitations, weakly specified methodology, ambiguous rules, cross-section evidence, unsupported layout requirements and adversarial embedded instructions. Confirm ground-truth semantics with the supervisor or a qualified reviewer. Do not assume the two student annotators alone establish scientific correctness.
